title: Chapter 25 — Postscript
paragraphs: In defense of the dignity of whaling, I would prefer to offer nothing but proven facts. But when an advocate has marshaled his facts, wouldn't it be wrong to suppress an entirely reasonable speculation that might speak powerfully in support of his case?

It is well known that at the coronation of kings and queens, even modern ones, a certain curious seasoning process is performed on them. There is a ceremonial salt cellar, and possibly a ceremonial spice shaker. How exactly they use the salt — who knows? What I am certain of, however, is that a king's head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, just like a head of lettuce being dressed for salad. Could it be that they anoint it to make the interior run smoothly, the way one oils machinery? Much could be said here about the essential dignity of this royal process, because in ordinary life we look down on anyone who oils his hair and obviously smells of it. In truth, a grown man who uses hair oil, unless for medical reasons, probably has a soft spot in him somewhere. As a general rule, he can't amount to much overall.

But the only question to consider here is this: what kind of oil is used at coronations? It certainly can't be olive oil, or macassar oil, or castor oil, or bear's grease, or train oil, or cod liver oil. What then can it possibly be, but sperm oil in its pure, unprocessed state — the finest of all oils?
Think about that, you loyal Britons! We whalemen supply your kings and queens with coronation oil!
